chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated from al-Abbas ibn Aamir ibn Rabah al-Thaqafi, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from al-Zurara ibn A'yun, who said: I heard Abu Abdullah saying:

A caller will call out from the Heaven: 'So-and-so is the Emir.' And another caller will call out: 'Ali and his followers are the triumphants.' I said: 'Then who will fight al-Mahdi after this?' He said: 'The Satan will call out: So-and-so and his followers are the triumphants (a man of the Umayyads).' I said: 'Then who will know the truthful from the liar?' He said: 'Those who used to narrate our traditions and said that he would come before he actually came, will know, and they will know that they are the truthful ones.'

key_terms.الشَّيْطَان: Satan, who creates confusion by announcing a rival
key_terms.الْحَدِيث: Traditions or narrations of the Imams
key_terms.الْفَائِزُونَ: The Triumphants, a title for Ali and his followers
key_terms.الْمَهْدِي: The Guided One, referring to the twelfth Imam
key_terms.بَنِي أُمَيَّة: The Umayyads, referring to the rival caliphate

ai.seo_question: How will people distinguish the true Mahdi from false claimants before his appearance?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Nu'mani’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* details the eschatological confusion preceding the Mahdi's appearance, where Satan incites a rival claimant, specifically noted as being from the Umayyad lineage, to challenge the true Imam. The hadith emphasizes that authentic knowledge of the Imams' traditions serves as the criterion for distinguishing truth from falsehood, a concept central to Shia epistemology regarding the continuity of guidance. This highlights the role of the 'those who narrate our hadith' as the discerning community that recognizes the Mahdi amidst the deceptive noise of the end times.
